title: ‘This is another freedom struggle to protect the Constitution’: K C Venugopal
content: After leading the freedom struggle and coming to power, the Congress had little reason to take to the streets in protest. Decades in government gradually dulled its agitational instincts, leaving a party more accustomed to wielding power than challenging it. Now, 12 years after losing power at the Centre, the grand old party is rediscovering the streets, entering one of the most protest-intensive phases in its post-Independence history. At the heart of this revival are two leaders who play distinctly different but complementary roles. Rahul Gandhi provides the energy and public face of the Congress's street politics, while K C Venugopal is the organisational force steering the movement, coordinating its campaigns and keeping the party machinery in motion. Venugopal's own journey into agitational politics has its roots in a defining episode in 1989. As president of the Kerala Students Union (KSU), he was brutally assaulted at the Nandavanam police camp, an incident that became a turning point in his political career. Nearly four decades later, the man who was once at the receiving end of police brutality is helping lead and coordinate the INDIA bloc's protests across the country. Venugopal has also acquired the unenviable distinction of being held accountable for every Congress defeat, wherever it occurs. Even electoral victories do not always spare him criticism, an irony that has become part of his political journey. Since the days of V K Krishna Menon and A K Antony, few Malayali politicians have had such a visible presence in the corridors of national politics in Delhi. Venugopal took charge as the Congress's general secretary (organisation) in 2019, when the party was at one of its weakest points, struggling to recover from successive electoral defeats and its loss of power at the Centre. The picture had changed considerably by 2024. The Congress doubled its parliamentary strength compared with its 2019 tally, while the Bharat Jodo Yatra and a series of subsequent agitations helped restore its presence on the streets. In the intervening years, several other opposition parties had lost steam, while the Congress increasingly positioned itself as the platform around which the opposition could rally. Today, the party is seeking to reclaim its role not merely as the principal opposition but also as a force capable of bringing together diverse political groups, accommodating their differences and leading collective resistance. Much of the organisational work behind this transformation has fallen to Venugopal. In this conversation, he discusses the Congress's return to protest politics, the challenges of holding the opposition together and his own engagement with the larger political battles shaping the country. Q. Will the Congress and the INDIA bloc succeed in achieving their goals? The Congress and the INDIA bloc are not fighting for some distant goal. The struggle itself is another freedom movement, a battle to protect the Constitution that made this country what it is and safeguard its constitutional institutions. And the struggle is already making headway. Several decisions taken by the Election Commission in response to our campaign bear testimony to this. The Commission decided that voters who could not be traced need not be summoned for hearings. It announced that the existing Form 6 could be used without modifications and launched an intensive drive to include voters left out of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process. It also barred the mass submission of Form 7 applications seeking the deletion of names from electoral rolls. A committee was constituted to audit the Commission's unified portal. The SIR exercise was announced in 17 States and Union Territories, while the process was extended in six others. The Commission also decided to provide political parties with soft copies of electoral rolls and dropped the requirement of an affidavit along with Form 6...
